issues.description: Pattern of nil-guarding every accessor instead of one IsZero check up front is bad taste
issues.detail: Look at this diff. Every single accessor on *File gets the same five-line ritual: declare a local var, check if f != nil, assign the field, then call the seq constructor on the local. That's eleven copies of the same special case. Good taste would be to either (a) have one helper that takes f and a field-extractor closure and does the nil-check once, or (b) make the underlying seq.NewFixedSlice tolerate a nil slice (which it already does — a nil slice has len 0) and just guard the field access. The current approach scales linearly with the number of accessors. Next person adding a getter will copy-paste this five-line pattern forever. That's the textbook special-case-instead-of-eliminate-special-case.

This commit is doing three different things: (1) adding a reflection-based zero-value test harness, (2) fixing nil-receiver panics on *File methods, (3) fixing IsZero panics on value-type methods (Type, Member, Oneof, Element, ReservedName, Symbol). Each of those should land independently with its own commit message explaining why. If the test harness has a bug, you cannot revert it without reverting the panic fixes. THREE-PATCHES.

issues.description: Inconsistent nil-discipline: some methods guard, some don't, no stated rule
issues.detail: File.IsDescriptorProto guards f == nil. File.InternedPath (called by IsDescriptorProto) apparently does not — at least it's not in this diff. File.FeatureSet guards. File.Deprecated does not appear to. There is no stated invariant for which *File methods are nil-safe and which aren't. Either ALL exported methods on *File tolerate nil, or NONE do and callers check. Pick one and document it at the type. Otherwise the next person reading this has to grep every method to know whether their call site is safe.

issues.description: DescriptorProto nil-guard is incomplete and papers over a real bug
issues.detail: imports.DescriptorProto guards i == nil but if i is non-nil with empty files, slicesx.Last returns the zero `imported`, and .file is nil — which is the intended behavior, fine. But Transitive does `i.files[:max(0, len(i.files)-1)]` which assumes the implicit descriptor.proto is always the last entry. If i.files is empty (which the nil-guard now permits because callers can construct a non-nil empty imports), the slice expression is fine but the semantic comment 'Exclude the implicit descriptor.proto' is a lie. State the invariant the type actually maintains.

issues.description: Reflection-based test harness is clever where a generated table would be obvious
issues.detail: The test walks methods via reflection, special-cases IsZero, ValueNodeIndex, Context by name string, and assumes any accessor with one input and >=1 outputs is fair game. This is the kind of test that silently stops checking something when a method gets renamed or a new accessor takes an argument. A boring table-driven test listing the methods explicitly would be longer but obvious. Acceptable as-is because it's a test and the failure mode is 'we stopped covering X' not 'production breaks', but flag it: the next person who adds a method with an unexported helper or a method that takes a context.Context will be confused why coverage silently dropped.

issues.description: ValueNodeIndex returning -1 for zero is an in-band error signal
issues.detail: Element.ValueNodeIndex now returns -1 for the zero value. The doc comment says 'If the element is empty, this returns -1'. This is the C-style sentinel pattern. Fine if the rest of the codebase consistently treats -1 as the not-found signal for indices, but the test then has to special-case this method by name. That's a smell: when the test has to know about method-specific return contracts, the contract is ad-hoc. Consider an (int, bool) signature or document the sentinel on the type, not just one method.

issues.description: Symbol.RawData zero-guard lives in export_test.go but the production Raw() path is unguarded
issues.detail: export_test.go now guards s.IsZero before calling s.Raw().data. That implies the unexported s.Raw() panics on zero. Fine for the test seam, but if Raw() panics on zero Symbol, that is a latent landmine for any other call site. Either Raw() should tolerate zero (return a zero rawSymbol pointer or similar) or the production callers should be audited. Adding the guard only in the test file fixes the test, not the underlying shape.

issues.description: Commit message tells us what, not why
issues.detail: PR description says 'Add a zero test ... similar to the one for the ast package ... It also fixes panics on zero values.' The why is buried. Why do we care about zero-value safety here — is the IR exposed in a public API where callers construct zero values? Is there a fuzzer hitting these paths? Is it for diagnostic code paths that handle partial parse failures? The maintainer six years from now reading `git blame` on these nil-guards will want the why. State it in the commit body.

review.summary: NEEDS-WORK. The intent is right — zero-value safety on a long-lived API is the kind of discipline a maintainer should welcome — and the test harness is a legitimate forcing function. But the execution shows bad taste: instead of eliminating the special case, the patch adds the same five-line nil-guard ritual eleven times across File. One helper or one rule (nil *File yields an empty seq) would replace all of it. This is the textbook example of writing a special case where you should have generalized. Also: this is three patches glued together (test harness, *File nil-safety, value-type IsZero-safety) and should land as three so any one can be reverted independently. Land it after a refactor pass on the File accessors and a split.
